claim: ABCA4 is a eukaryotic importer transporting retinal to the cytosol to enter the visual cycle.
source: ABCA4 is a eukaryotic importer transporting retinal to the cytosol to enter the visual cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of ABCA4, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: ABCA4 removes toxic retinoids from the disc lumen.
source: It also removes toxic retinoids from the disc lumen.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of ABCA4, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Mutations in ABCA4 cause impaired vision or blindness.
source: Mutations in ABCA4 cause impaired vision or blindness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by established clinical knowledge.

claim: In the absence of ATP, ABCA4 adopts an outward-facing conformation, poised to recruit substrate.
source: In the absence of ATP, ABCA4 adopts an outward-facing conformation, poised to recruit substrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of ATP induces large conformational changes in ABCA4 that could lead to substrate release.
source: The presence of ATP induces large conformational changes that could lead to substrate release.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural data presented in the manuscript, with speculative interpretation about substrate release.

claim: Over 800 mutations in the ABCA4 gene cause Stargardt disease, the most common form of inherited macular degeneration.
source: Over 800 mutations in the ABCA4 gene cause Stargardt disease, the most common form of inherited macular degeneration (Lin et al., 2016; Ran et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Age-related macular degeneration, autosomal-recessive retinitis pigmentosa, and cone-rod dystrophy are linked to defective ABCA4.
source: Several other diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, autosomal-recessive retinitis pigmentosa, and cone-rod dystrophy, are also linked to defective ABCA4 (Allikmets et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Currently, no cure nor effective treatment exists for ABCA4-related diseases.
source: Currently, no cure nor effective treatment exists for these diseases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the current state of treatment.

claim: The vast majority of eukaryotic ABC transporters are exporters.
source: In eukaryotes, however, the vast majority of ABC transporters are exporters.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ABC transporters.

claim: ABCA4 is an exception among eukaryotic ABC transporters, functioning as an importer in photoreceptor cells.
source: ABCA4 is an exception; it functions as an importer in photoreceptor cells, where light stimuli are translated into electric signals (Figure 1A; Illing et al., 1997; Papermaster et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Light catalyzes the isomerization of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal.
source: Light catalyzes the isomerization of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, which is subsequently released from the activated opsin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the visual cycle.

claim: ABCA4 enables the visual cycle by moving all-trans retinal into the cytoplasm, likely in the form of its phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) conjugates, N-retinylidene-PE.
source: ABCA4 enables this process by moving all-trans retinal into the cytoplasm, likely in the form of its phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) conjugates, N-retinylidene-PE (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and represents established understanding with some speculation about the form of transport.

claim: ABCA4 clears excess trans and 11-cis retinal out of the disc lumen to prevent potential toxicity.
source: In addition, ABCA4 also clears excess trans and 11-cis retinal out of the disc lumen to prevent potential toxicity (Quazi and Molday, 2014; Weng et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Retinoids bind to purified ABCA4 and stimulate its ATPase activity.
source: Retinoids have been shown to bind to purified ABCA4 and stimulate its ATPase activity (Ahn et al., 2000; Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ABCA4 actively transports N-retinylidene-PE across disc membranes.
source: Transporter assays have demonstrated that ABCA4 actively transports N-retinylidene-PE across disc membranes (Quazi et al., 2012; Quazi and Molday, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ABCA4 is an ATP-driven importer, transporting N-retinylidene-PE from the luminal to the cytoplasmic side of the disc membrane in photoreceptor cells.
source: These studies provide direct evidence that ABCA4 is an ATP-driven importer, transporting N-retinylidene-PE from the luminal to the cytoplasmic side of the disc membrane in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited studies.

claim: The overall architecture of bovine ABCA4 was characterized by electron microscopy to 18 Å resolution.
source: Previously, the overall architecture of bovine ABCA4 was characterized by electron microscopy (EM) to 18 Å resolution (Tsybovsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The structure of ABCA1 was determined to be 4.1 Å.
source: More recently, the structure of a related transporter, ABCA1, was determined to be 4.1 Å (Qian et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ABCA1 is a lipid exporter sharing 51% sequence identity with ABCA4 but transports substrate in the opposite direction.
source: ABCA1 is a lipid exporter sharing 51% sequence identity with ABCA4 but transports substrate in the opposite direction.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about ABCA1.

claim: The structures of human ABCA4 in two conformations were determined at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: These structures, both determined at 3.3 Å resolution, reveal ATP-dependent conformational changes different from those observed in any other ABC transporters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structures of ABCA4 reveal ATP-dependent conformational changes different from those observed in any other ABC transporters.
source: These structures, both determined at 3.3 Å resolution, reveal ATP-dependent conformational changes different from those observed in any other ABC transporters.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The E1087 and E2096 residues are conserved as the general bases catalyzing ATP hydrolysis.
source: The E1087 and E2096 residues were conserved as the general bases catalyzing ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these conserved residues.

claim: Mutation of the corresponding residues to E1087 and E2096 in many other ABC transporters abolished ATP hydrolysis but not ATP binding.
source: Mutation of the corresponding residues in many other ABC transporters abolished ATP hydrolysis but not ATP binding (Kim and Chen, 2018; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The size-exclusion profiles of the purified EQ mutant and the WT protein are comparable, suggesting that the EQ mutant folds similarly to the WT protein.
source: The size-exclusion profiles of the purified EQ mutant and the WT protein are comparable, suggesting that the EQ mutant folds similarly to the WT protein (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 1B with inference about protein folding.

claim: The recombinant WT ABCA4 shows a Km of 80 ± 10 µM for ATP.
source: The recombinant WT protein shows a Km of 80 ± 10 µM for ATP and a maximal hydrolysis activity of 28.1 ± 0.7 ATP per minute (or 112.5 ± 2.8 nmol/mg/min), comparable to those of the native protein purified from rod photoreceptor cells (75 ± 18 µM and 190 ± 36 nmol/mg/min, respectively) (Ahn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATPase activity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The recombinant WT ABCA4 shows a maximal hydrolysis activity of 28.1 ± 0.7 ATP per minute (or 112.5 ± 2.8 nmol/mg/min).
source: The recombinant WT protein shows a Km of 80 ± 10 µM for ATP and a maximal hydrolysis activity of 28.1 ± 0.7 ATP per minute (or 112.5 ± 2.8 nmol/mg/min), comparable to those of the native protein purified from rod photoreceptor cells (75 ± 18 µM and 190 ± 36 nmol/mg/min, respectively) (Ahn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATPase activity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The recombinant WT ABCA4 has comparable ATPase activity to the native protein purified from rod photoreceptor cells.
source: The recombinant WT protein shows a Km of 80 ± 10 µM for ATP and a maximal hydrolysis activity of 28.1 ± 0.7 ATP per minute (or 112.5 ± 2.8 nmol/mg/min), comparable to those of the native protein purified from rod photoreceptor cells (75 ± 18 µM and 190 ± 36 nmol/mg/min, respectively) (Ahn et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data with cited literature values.

claim: The EQ mutant shows no measurable ATPase activity.
source: The EQ mutant, on the other hand, shows no measurable ATPase activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the presence of PE, retinal stimulates the ATPase activity of WT ABCA4 by up to threefold.
source: Also consistent with literature (Quazi and Molday, 2014), in the presence of PE, retinal stimulates the ATPase activity of WT ABCA4 by up to threefold (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 1D, consistent with cited literature.

claim: No stimulation of ATPase activity was observed with retinoic acid or in the absence of PE.
source: No stimulation was observed with retinoic acid or in the absence of PE (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The recombinant ABCA4 exhibits biochemical properties very similar to the ABCA4 purified from native sources.
source: These data indicate that the recombinant ABCA4 exhibits biochemical properties very similar to the ABCA4 purified from native sources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of experimental data with literature values.

claim: Human ABCA4 is a single polypeptide of 2273 residues.
source: The human ABCA4 is a single polypeptide of 2273 residues (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about ABCA4 structure, referenced to Figure 2.

claim: ABCA4 consists of two homologous halves, each containing a transmembrane domain (TMD), an exocytoplasmic domain (ECD), a cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domain (NBD), and a regulatory domain (RD).
source: It consists of two homologous halves, each containing a transmembrane domain (TMD), an exocytoplasmic domain (ECD), a cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domain (NBD), and a regulatory domain (RD) (Bungert et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ABCA4 structure, supported by a citation.

claim: The structure of WT ABCA4 was determined by single-molecule cryo-EM in the absence of ATP and substrate to an overall resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: The structure of WT ABCA4 was determined by single-molecule cryo-EM in the absence of ATP and substrate to an overall resolution of 3.3 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EM density of ABCA4 is of high quality, permitting de novo building of most residues, except for a few loops and a 134-residue region in ECD1.
source: The EM density is of high quality (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), permitting de novo building of most residues, except for a few loops and a 134-residue region in ECD1 (Figure 2B, blue density).
evidence: This is a description of the quality of the cryo-EM data and model building.

claim: Residues 118–137 and 479–496 were built as polyalanine as their side chain densities were invisible.
source: In addition, residues 118–137 and 479–496 were built as polyalanine as their side chain densities were invisible.
evidence: This is a description of the model building process based on the quality of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The final model of WT ABCA4 consists of 1941 residues, 14 lipids, 1 detergent molecule, and 14 sugar molecules.
source: The final model, consisting of 1941 residues, 14 lipids, 1 detergent molecule, and 14 sugar molecules, was refined to excellent stereochemistry (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the final structural model.

claim: ABCA4 is an elongated molecule, extending approximately 240 Å across the lipid bilayer.
source: ABCA4 is an elongated molecule, extending approximately 240 Å across the lipid bilayer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two ECDs of ABCA4 pack closely with each other, protruding 130 Å into the lumen.
source: The two ECDs pack closely with each other, protruding 130 Å into the lumen (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two TMDs of ABCA4 adopt an outward-facing configuration, forming a large hydrophobic cavity that is continuous with both the luminal solution and, through a lateral opening, to the lipid bilayer itself.
source: The two TMDs adopt an outward-facing configuration, forming a large hydrophobic cavity that is continuous with both the luminal solution and, through a lateral opening, to the lipid bilayer itself.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the absence of ATP, the two NBDs of ABCA4 are apart from each other and the two RDs form extensive interdomain interactions.
source: In the absence of ATP, the two NBDs are apart from each other and the two RDs form extensive interdomain interactions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The highly specific localization of ABCA4 to the rim region of the disc membrane might be due to the large size of the ECD domains.
source: It was previously suggested that the highly specific localization of ABCA4 to the rim region of the disc membrane (Figure 1A) might be due to the large size of the ECD domains (Molday, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on a previous suggestion cited from literature.

claim: The structure of ABCA4 supports the notion that the spacing between the flattened regions of the disc membranes may be insufficient to accommodate the elongated ECDs.
source: The structure of ABCA4 supports this notion as the spacing between the flattened regions of the disc membranes (Nickell et al., 2007) may be insufficient to accommodate the elongated ECDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and cited literature about disc membrane spacing.

claim: The luminal region of ABCA4 is composed of 600 residues in ECD1 and 290 residues in ECD2.
source: The luminal region, composed of 600 residues in ECD1 and 290 residues in ECD2, does not contain any known enzymatic or structural motifs of known function.
evidence: This is a description of the structural composition based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The luminal region of ABCA4 does not contain any known enzymatic or structural motifs of known function.
source: The luminal region, composed of 600 residues in ECD1 and 290 residues in ECD2, does not contain any known enzymatic or structural motifs of known function.
evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis and comparison with known motifs.

claim: More than 300 disease-causing mutations map to the ECD region of ABCA4.
source: However, more than 300 disease-causing mutations map to this region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Human Gene Mutations Database: http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk), underscoring the essential nature of the ECDs.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the Human Gene Mutations Database.

claim: The ECDs of ABCA4 assemble to form one unit with a large extended hollow interior, accessible from the luminal space.
source: Instead, the ECDs assemble to form one unit with a large extended hollow interior, accessible from the luminal space (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The structure of the ECDs can be separated into three layers: base, tunnel, and lid.
source: The structure, as previously described for ABCA1 (Qian et al., 2017), can be separated into three layers: base, tunnel, and lid (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the structural organization, with reference to a similar description for ABCA1.

claim: The tunnel of the ECDs is an α-helical barrel with an inner diameter of approximately 15 Å.
source: The tunnel is an -helical barrel with an inner diameter of approximately 15 Å (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The density corresponding to the lid region does not permit amino acid assignment, suggesting that the lid region is flexible.
source: The density corresponding to the lid region does not permit amino acid assignment, suggesting that the lid region is flexible (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quality of the cryo-EM density.

claim: Strong densities that may correspond to lipid or detergent molecules were observed inside the extended groove in the base layer of the ECDs.
source: Strong densities that may correspond to lipid or detergent molecules were observed inside the extended groove in the base layer (Figure 3A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density with speculative interpretation.

claim: The structure of the ECDs is stabilized by six disulfide bonds.
source: Consistent with biochemical analysis (Bungert et al., 2001), the structure of the ECDs is stabilized by six disulfide bonds (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with cited biochemical analysis.

claim: Seven missense mutations of the cysteines involved in disulfide bonding (C54Y, C75G, C519R, C641S, C1455R, C1488R, and C1490Y) have been identified in patients with retinal diseases.
source: Seven missense mutations of the cysteines involved in disulfide bonding (C54Y, C75G, C519R, C641S, C1455R, C1488R, and C1490Y) have been identified in patients with retinal diseases (Fumagalli et al., 2001; Hu et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 1999; Rosenberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Densities corresponding to sugar moieties were observed on residues N98, N415, N444, N504, N1469, N1529, N1588, and N1662 of ABCA4.
source: Densities corresponding to sugar moieties were observed on residues N98, N415, N444, N504, N1469, N1529, N1588, and N1662.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: Glycosylation likely plays an important role in the folding or trafficking of ABCA4.
source: It is likely that glycosylation plays an important role in the folding or trafficking of ABCA4,as missense mutations at positions 415, 504, and 1588 are linked to retinal diseases (Consugar et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of disease-causing mutations at glycosylation sites.

claim: Prokaryotic ABC importers often contain an extracytoplasmic binding protein that functions as a receptor for substrates.
source: Prokaryotic ABC importers often contain an extracytoplasmic binding protein that functions as a receptor for substrates (Davidson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about prokaryotic ABC importers, supported by a citation.

claim: It is currently unknown if the ECDs of ABCA4 have an analogous function to the extracytoplasmic binding protein in prokaryotic ABC importers.
source: Currently it is unknown if the ECDs of ABCA4 have an analogous function.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Isolated ECD2 binds to all-trans retinal.
source: Previously it was shown that isolated ECD2 binds to all-trans retinal (Biswas-Fiss et al., 2010), but how this interaction relates to the transport cycle remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: How the interaction between ECD2 and all-trans retinal relates to the transport cycle remains unclear.
source: Previously it was shown that isolated ECD2 binds to all-trans retinal (Biswas-Fiss et al., 2010), but how this interaction relates to the transport cycle remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: The structure of the TMD of ABCA4 belongs to the newly classified type V fold.
source: The structure of the TMD belongs to the newly classified type V fold (Thomas and Tampé, 2020) previously observed only in ABC exporters (Lee et al., 2016; Qian et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2017; Bi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a classification based on structural comparison with cited literature.

claim: The two TMDs of ABCA4 come in contact with each other through two helical turns at the cytoplasmic end of TM5 and TM11, burying only 124 Å² surface per subunit.
source: The two TMDs come in contact with each other through two helical turns at the cytoplasmic end of TM5 and TM11, burying only 124 2 surface per subunit (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The gap between the TMDs at the level of the inner leaflet is filled with ordered lipids.
source: The gap between the TMDs at the level of the inner leaflet is filled with ordered lipids (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The cytoplasmic gate of the transmembrane pathway is formed partially by residues in TM5 and TM11 and partially by lipid molecules.
source: Thus, the cytoplasmic gate of the transmembrane pathway is formed partially by residues in TM5 and TM11 and partially by lipid molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Mutations of many lipid-interacting residues are found in patients with vision diseases.
source: Mutations of many lipid-interacting residues are found in patients with vision diseases (Human Gene Mutations Database: http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the Human Gene Mutations Database.

claim: Lipids form an integral part of the retinoid transport system, possibly by regulating the folding and function of ABCA4.
source: These observations indicate that lipids form an integral part of the retinoid transport system, possibly by regulating the folding and function of ABCA4 (Figure 1, Ahn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and cited literature, with speculative interpretation.

claim: Each TMD of ABCA4 contains two exocytoplasmic helices (EHs) forming a EH-turn-EH insertion halfway into the membrane.
source: A prominent feature of the type V fold is that each TMD contains two exocytoplasmic helices (EHs) forming a EH-turn-EH insertion halfway into the membrane (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each EH of ABCA4 exposes a helical end to the low dielectric membrane center, a thermodynamically unfavorable configuration.
source: Each EH exposes a helical end to the low dielectric membrane center, a thermodynamically unfavorable configuration.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and thermodynamic principles.

claim: In TMD1 of ABCA4, D846 and Y850 form hydrogen bonds with mainchain carbonyl oxygen and amide atoms of EH1 and EH2, respectively.
source: In TMD1, D846 and Y850 form hydrogen bonds with mainchain carbonyl oxygen and amide atoms of EH1 and EH2, respectively (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In TMD2 of ABCA4, E1885 and Y1889 neutralize the ionizable atoms at the ends of EH3 and EH4.
source: In TMD2, E1885 and Y1889 neutralize the ionizable atoms at the ends of EH3 and EH4 (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutating E1885 to lysine causes Stargardt disease, likely due to folding defects.
source: Mutating E1885 to lysine causes Stargardt disease (Rivera et al., 2000), likely due to folding defects.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature with speculative interpretation about the mechanism.

claim: The EH3-turn-EH4 insertion leads to a large hydrophilic cleft on the surface of TMD2.
source: The EH3-turn-EH4 insertion leads to a large hydrophilic cleft on the surface of TMD2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A cluster of charged residues from EH3, EH4, and TM12, including the clinically relevant residue R1843, are located as deep as 10 Å below the expected membrane surface.
source: A cluster of charged residues from EH3, EH4, and TM12, including the clinically relevant residue R1843 (Lewis et al., 1999; Rivera et al., 2000), are located as deep as 10 below the expected membrane surface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure, with reference to clinical relevance from cited literature.

claim: In some K+ or Cl- channels, helices with one end exposed to the membrane contribute to the binding and selection of conducting ions.
source: In some K+ or Cl- channels, helices with one end exposed to the membrane contribute to the binding and selection of conducting ions (Doyle, 1998; Faraldo-Gómez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ion channels, supported by citations.

claim: The functional significance of the EH-turn-EH insertion motif in type V transporters is still unknown.
source: Although the EH-turn-EH insertion is highly conserved in type V transporters, the functional significance of this motif is still unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: In the cytoplasm of ABCA4, the two NBDs and two RDs form a domain-swapped dimer.
source: In the cytoplasm, the two NBDs and two RDs form a domain-swapped dimer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: RD1 crosses the dimer interface to interact with NBD2, and RD2 crosses back over to pack against NBD1.
source: RD1 crosses the dimer interface to interact with NBD2, and RD2 crosses back over to pack against NBD1.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The two RDs of ABCA4 have very similar structures; both exhibit a fold similar to the ACT domain.
source: The two RDs have very similar structures; both exhibit a fold similar to the ACT domain (Figure 4D), which is a conserved structural motif that typically binds small regulatory molecules (Chipman and Shaanan, 2001; Grant, 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure, with reference to the known function of ACT domains from cited literature.

claim: The ACT domain is a conserved structural motif that typically binds small regulatory molecules.
source: The two RDs have very similar structures; both exhibit a fold similar to the ACT domain (Figure 4D), which is a conserved structural motif that typically binds small regulatory molecules (Chipman and Shaanan, 2001; Grant, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ACT domains, supported by citations.

claim: The ACT fold is conserved among all members of the ABCA subfamily.
source: Sequence alignment indicates that the ACT fold is conserved among all members of the ABCA subfamily (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence alignment analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The bacterial methionine importer MetNI contains two RDs with ACT-like folds.
source: In the ABC transporter superfamily, the bacterial methionine importer MetNI also contains two RDs with ACT-like folds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MetNI.

claim: The RDs of MetNI play an important role in 'trans-inhibition': at high intracellular concentration, methionine binds to the RDs to inhibit further uptake of methionine.
source: The RDs of MetNI play an important role in 'trans-inhibition': at high intracellular concentration, methionine binds to the RDs to inhibit further uptake of methionine (Kadaba et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: An NBD1-R1 construct of ABCA4 binds retinal with high affinity.
source: For ABCA4, it was reported that an NBD1-R1 construct binds retinal with high affinity (Biswas-Fiss et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Whether retinal binding to ABCA4 is mediated through the ACT motif and the physiological relevance of such interaction remain to be investigated.
source: Whether retinal binding is mediated through the ACT motif and the physiological relevance of such interaction remain to be investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: The structure of the hydrolysis-deficient mutant ABCA4-EQ was determined in the presence of 10 mM ATP-Mg2+ to 3.3 Å resolution.
source: To capture ABCA4 in its ATP-bound state, the structure of the hydrolysis-deficient mutant ABCA4-EQ was determined in the presence of 10 mM ATP-Mg2+ to 3.3 Å resolution (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both 2D and 3D image classes from cryo-EM data show that most particles of ABCA4-EQ are in the NBD-dimerized configuration.
source: Both 2D and 3D image classes from cryo-EM data show that most particles are in the NBD-dimerized configuration.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The final model of ABCA4-EQ contains 2 ATP molecules, 8 lipid molecules, and 1920 residues.
source: The final model contains 2 ATP molecules, 8 lipid molecules, and 1920 residues.
evidence: This is a description of the final structural model.

claim: Similar to that of the WT protein, the lid region of ABCA4-EQ is highly mobile.
source: Similar to that of the WT protein, the lid region is highly mobile.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quality of the cryo-EM density.

claim: In the presence of ATP and absence of substrate, ABCA4 exhibits a conformation very different from that of the ATP-free structure.
source: In the presence of ATP and absence of substrate, ABCA4 exhibits a conformation very different from that of the ATP-free structure (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparison of the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: In the ATP-bound state, the two NBDs of ABCA4 form a closed dimer.
source: The two NBDs form a closed dimer.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the ATP-bound cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the ATP-bound state, the two TMDs of ABCA4 are in close contact, leaving no cavity at their interface.
source: The two TMDs are also in close contact, leaving no cavity at their interface (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the ATP-bound cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the ATP-bound state, the ECDs of ABCA4 are positioned differently from that of the ATP-free form, placing the hollow channel directly above the EH3-turn-EH4 cleft.
source: The ECDs are positioned differently from that of the ATP-free form, placing the hollow channel directly above the EH3-turn-EH4 cleft (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the ATP-bound cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ATP-binding signature motifs of ABCA4 deviate from the consensus LSGGQ sequence.
source: The ATP-binding signature motifs of ABCA4 deviate from the consensus LSGGQ sequence.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: The signature motif of NBD1 is LSGGM and that of NBD2 is YSGGN.
source: The signature motif of NBD1 is LSGGM and that of NBD2 is YSGGN.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: In a typical ATPase site, Q in the LSGGQ signature motif positions the ribose moiety of ATP through an H-bond and van der Waals' contact.
source: In a typical ATPase site, Q in the LSGGQ signature motif positions the ribose moiety of ATP through an H-bond and van der Waals' contact (Davidson and Chen, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about typical ATPase sites, supported by a citation.

claim: In ABCA4, the role of Q in positioning the ribose moiety is fulfilled by the mainchain carboxyl group of T2070 in ATPase site 1 and the side chain of K1054 and mainchain carboxyl of D1061 in ATPase site 2.

claim: The resting state of ABCA4 is outward-facing, in opposing contrast to typical ABC transporters that are inward-facing when their NBDs are separated.
source: In opposing contrast to typical ABC transporters that are inward-facing when their NBDs are separated, the resting state of ABCA4 is outward-facing (Figure 2).

claim: The nature of the conformational change in ABCA4 is qualitatively different from the 'rocker-switch' motion described for many transporters.

claim: Transition from the ATP-free to ATP-bound conformation involves two motions of the TMDs: a movement in concert with the NBDs toward the molecular center, and a 30° twisting motion of TMD1 relative to the RecA-like subdomain.

claim: The helical subdomain of NBD1 moves together with TMD1 during the conformational change.
